meta.title: Maths Map - Level 2 Item Bank (Draft for parent review)
meta.curriculumSource: Victorian Curriculum F-10 (2.0) Mathematics, Level 2. Codes are © VCAA, CC-BY-NC 3.0.

scoring.notes: choice/order items: correct = 2, otherwise 0. observe items: parent uses rubric to award 0/1/2.

itemTypes.order: Child taps items into the correct sequence
itemTypes.observe: Parent-led task with household materials; parent ticks secure / partial / not yet using the rubric

items.prompt: What number comes right after 899?
Tap the numbers from smallest to biggest:
Which number is BIGGER: 385 or 358?
Which is the smallest? 808, 880, 818, 881
Ordering three-digit numbers with explanation
items.observeScript: Write 5 different three-digit numbers on cards (e.g. 333, 353, 533, 303, 530), shuffle, and ask your child to order them from smallest to biggest. Then ask: 'How did you know which was which?' Listen for place-value reasoning (hundreds first, then tens, then ones).

observeRubric.secure: Orders all five correctly AND explains using hundreds/tens/ones (e.g. '533 is bigger because 5 hundreds beats 3 hundreds')
observeRubric.partial: Orders most correctly, reasoning shaky or relies on digit-guessing
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot order reliably or uses no comparison strategy

items.prompt: 245 is the same as…
307 — what does the 0 in the middle tell us?
Rename 245 as tens and ones.
35 ones + 2 hundreds = ?
Renaming a three-digit number three ways
items.observeScript: Give your child a number like 326 (or use pasta/coins). Ask them to show it three ways: (1) 3 hundreds, 2 tens, 6 ones, (2) 32 tens and 6 ones, (3) 3 hundreds and 26 ones. If you have bundles of 10 craft sticks, use them; or just say it aloud and watch how they decompose it.

observeRubric.secure: Produces all three renames correctly, including the non-standard ones
observeRubric.partial: Produces the standard partition (3/2/6) and one other, with prompting
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot rename beyond the hundreds/tens/ones reading

items.prompt: A pizza is cut into 4 EQUAL slices. One slice is called…
Half of 12 is…
Which is BIGGER: one-half or one-quarter?
If you fold a strip of paper in half, then fold it in half AGAIN, how many equal parts do you get?
Repeated halving with paper
items.observeScript: Give your child a long strip of paper. Say: 'Fold it in half — how many equal parts?' (Slash fold, name it 'one-half'). 'Open it, fold it in half again — how many now?' (quarters). 'Again?' (eighths). Ask: 'Which part is biggest? Which is smallest? A quarter is a half of what?' (a half).

observeRubric.secure: Names halves, quarters, eighths; explains quarter = half of a half; compares sizes correctly
observeRubric.partial: Counts parts correctly but shaky naming or comparing
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot track the halving or connect the sizes

items.prompt: You were given a $100 gift card and spent $38. How much is left?
Solving a two-step money problem with a number sentence
items.observeScript: Name the situation: 'You had $100 in a gift card. You bought shoes for $38 and a T-shirt for $15. How much money is left on the card?' Ask your child to solve it any way they like, then write the number sentence on paper, and explain what each part means. Encourage any strategy: counting back, subtracting tens then ones, or number line jumps.

observeRubric.secure: Gives $47 with a sensible strategy and a number sentence that matches the situation
observeRubric.partial: Gets $47 with heavy support or a fuzzy number sentence (right answer, can't yet explain it)
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot set up or solve; guessing

items.prompt: There are 4 trays and 6 biscuits on each tray. How many biscuits in total?
How many dots in a '3 fives' array (3 rows of 5)?
Share $36 equally between 4 people. How much does each person get?
Which of these is NOT a way to make 12?
Sharing vs grouping — same numbers, different question
items.observeScript: Round 1: 'Here are 24 counters. Share them equally between 4 plates.' (6 each). Round 2: 'Same 24 counters. Make groups of 4.' (6 groups). Then ask: 'Are those the same problem, or different?' Watch whether they notice both are about 24 and 4, but one is about making plates, one is about making groups.

observeRubric.secure: Completes both correctly AND can say what is same/different (quotition vs partition)
observeRubric.partial: Completes both but can't yet compare them

items.prompt: 'Each of the 25 kids in class brings $2. How much money will we have in total?' — which operation solves this?
You buy 3 books at $5 each. How much do you spend in total?
We are making teams of 4. There are 16 kids. How many teams?
You had $50. You spent $23. How much money is left?
The family fundraiser
items.observeScript: Play money: pretend the whole family (you, child, 2 siblings/cousins or toys) each gives $2 to the school fundraiser. Ask: 'How much will the family give in total?' Then: 'If we save $5 each week for 4 weeks, how much will we have saved?' Let them use coins, drawings, skip counting or any strategy. Finish by asking them to choose a way to SHOW the problem (drawing, number sentence).

observeRubric.secure: Solves both with a chosen strategy and can show/record the problem
observeRubric.partial: Solves one fluently, the other with support

items.prompt: What comes next? 3, 5, 7, 9, …
What comes next? 20, 17, 14, …
Pattern: keep adding 3. 4, 7, 10, __. What is the missing number?
Matchstick triangles grow: 3, 5, 7… What is the rule?
Building an additive pattern and finding the rule
items.observeScript: With blocks or pasta: build 'one triangle of matchsticks, two triangles sharing a side…' or simpler — towers of 2, 4, 6, 8 cubes. Ask your child: 'What is happening each time? What comes next? What would the 6th tower look like?' Then swap: THEY make up a pattern for you to guess.

observeRubric.secure: States the constant increase/decrease, predicts further terms, and invents a working pattern
observeRubric.partial: Extends the pattern by one or two steps but can't state the constant rule
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot continue or describe the pattern

items.prompt: Ten-frames and related subtraction facts
items.observeScript: Use ten-frames (or draw them): show 7 + 8 as two frames filled (one full frame + 7, another full frame +... ). Ask: 'What is 7 + 8?' Then: 'If 8 + 7 = 15, what is 15 − 7? What is 15 − 8?' See whether they connect the family of facts instead of counting from zero.

observeRubric.secure: Says 7+8=15, 15−7=8 and 15−8=7, linked to the ten-frame
observeRubric.partial: Gets the addition but must re-derive subtraction by counting
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot hold or connect the fact family yet

items.prompt: Double 6 = ?
Half of 16 is…
If double 9 = 18, then 18 ÷ 2 = ?
Double-or-halve race
items.observeScript: Roll a die (or pick numbers aloud from 2 to 12). Your child chooses: DOUBLE it or HALVE it. Goal: reach exactly 24 (start anywhere under 24, or your call). Example turns: 6 → double → 12 → double → 24 ✓. Play 3 rounds. Watch whether doubling/halving comes fluently or needs counting.

observeRubric.secure: Doubles/halves numbers to 20 instantly in the game, chooses strategy freely
observeRubric.partial: Correct but slow/count-based; needs a bit of support mid-game
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot reliably halve, or doubling is fragile

items.prompt: '3 groups of 4 counters' is the same as…
12 − 3 − 3 − 3 − 3 = 0. How many times did we subtract 3?
Which number sentence matches 'shared 12 into 4 equal groups'?
Every way to split 15 into equal groups
items.observeScript: Give 15 counters. Ask: 'How many equal groups can you make with these? Show me as many ways as you can.' They should find: 15×1, 5×3, 3×5 (and maybe 15 = 3+3+3+3+3). For each, ask them to write the number sentence. If they find only one or two, nudge with 'what about groups of 5?'

observeRubric.secure: Finds 1×15/3×5/5×3 and writes a number sentence for each
observeRubric.partial: Finds 2 of them, or finds them but can't write the sentence

items.prompt: To measure your friend's height ACCURATELY, should you use hand spans or finger widths?
Maya measured the desk as '12 shoes-lengths'. Sam measured it as '8 steps'. Why did they get different numbers?
You want to know WHICH of 3 containers holds the MOST sand. What should you do?
options: Compare by pouring one into another

items.prompt: Same unit, same object — but your measurement is 14 and mum's is 7. Most likely cause?
Choosing bigger or smaller units wisely
items.observeScript: Ask your child to measure the length of the lounge rug (or bed) three times: (1) in whole footsteps, (2) in toy-car lengths, (3) in paperclips end-to-end. Compare the numbers: 'Why is the paperclip number bigger than the footsteps number?' They should see: smaller units → bigger count → more accurate.

observeRubric.secure: Measures with all 3 units and says WHY smaller units give a bigger count
observeRubric.partial: Measures fine but can't articulate the smaller-units-more-accuracy idea
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot handle end-to-end measurement with uniform units yet

items.prompt: One-quarter of an hour is how many minutes?
'Quarter past two' means what time?
Fold a paper in half, then in half again. How many equal parts?
Which is MORE of a cup of water: half or quarter?
Kitchen halves and quarters
items.observeScript: Get a set of measuring cups/spoons if you have them (or two identical cups + one small glass). Ask: 'If one cup fills the glass, how much is half a cup? Show me with the small glass.' Then: 'And quarter of a cup?' If no cups, use a sandwich: 'Cut it in half. Now half again?'

observeRubric.secure: Identifies half and quarter accurately with real objects, using the words properly
observeRubric.partial: Gets half; quarter is shaky or they halve wrongly
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot halve or quarter objects/quantities yet

items.prompt: Today is March 3. What date is it 10 days from now?
How many days are there in a weekend (Saturday and Sunday)?
Your birthday is June 12. Today is June 5. How many days until your birthday?
Which date comes FIRST: May 5 or May 15?
Calendar detective
items.observeScript: Use a real calendar (kitchen one is perfect). Ask: 'Find your birthday. How many days from today is it?' 'What day was it June 5 / will it be June 20?' 'Find AN already-passed event we went to — count the days since it.' Note if they use fingers to count, jumps of 7 days, or a mental strategy.

observeRubric.secure: Finds dates freely, counts days between events correctly using the calendar
observeRubric.partial: Counts but loses track; needs reminding of how to count 2-week jumps
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot use a calendar to find dates or count days between

items.prompt: Minute hand on the 6, hour hand just past the 3 — what time is it?
'Quarter past' means how many minutes past the hour?
Half past seven is the same as…
Quarter TO 4 is the same as…
Paper-plate clock
items.observeScript: Make a clock together (paper plate, write 1-12, add 2 hands — one long, one short). Ask your child to show: 3:00, 7:30, 9:15 and 5:45. After each, ask: 'Where does the SHORT hand point? Where does the LONG hand point? How do you know?'

observeRubric.secure: Sets all four times correctly, explains both hands' jobs and the quarter/half positions
observeRubric.partial: Hour times fine, half/quarter times shaky or swapped
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot set a clock to even the hour reliably

items.prompt: How many QUARTER turns make a FULL turn (all the way around)?
A HALF turn the same as how many quarter turns?
Turn left, turn left, turn left, turn left. Where do you end up facing?
Three-quarter turn = how many quarter turns?
Turn dance
items.observeScript: Clear some floor space. Call out: 'quarter turn!' (they spin a quarter), 'half turn!', 'full turn!', 'three-quarter turn!'. Then reverse: they call, you turn. Then find things at home that turn half a turn (tap handle, door knob, peanut butter lid) and work out what kind of turn each is.

observeRubric.secure: Responds correctly to all four calls, turns in both directions, and names turns at home

items.prompt: Which of these shapes has exactly 4 sides?
Parallel lines are lines that…
options: never meet, however far they go

items.prompt: Which shape has ONLY curved sides?
If you turn a triangle upside-down, what stays the same?
options: its size and number of sides

items.prompt: Sorting shapes by a rule you choose
items.observeScript: Give a mixed bag: circles, ovals, triangles, squares, rectangles, pentagons (cut out or drawn). Ask: 'Sort these into TWO groups.' Whatever they choose, ask: 'What is your rule?' Then push once more: 'Can you sort them a DIFFERENT way?' (e.g. by sides, by curved/straight, by parallel sides or not).

observeRubric.secure: Sorts at least two different ways and states rules using formal spatial terms (sides, straight, curved, parallel)
observeRubric.partial: Sorts one way; second way needs prompting or vocabulary is missing
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot sort by any consistent rule

items.prompt: In a seating plan, 'front row, third seat' means…
On most maps, which direction is at the TOP?
What does 'forward two squares' mean?
You follow directions: 'forward, right, forward, right'. How many turns do you make?
Grid treasure hunt on the floor
items.observeScript: Make a 4×4 grid on the floor (tape, chalk, or big paper with gridlines). Hide a small toy under one square. You give directions FROM the corner: 'forward one, right one, forward two…' until they find it. Then they give YOU directions from a different corner to find it again. Note how precise their left/right/forward/back language is.

observeRubric.secure: Gives and follows 4–5 step directions; left/right consistent; says what each step means
observeRubric.partial: Follows yours fine, but their own directions are vague ('go there') or left/right shaky
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot follow a 3-step path or give any useful directions

items.prompt: Which is the BEST question for a class survey?
When planning a survey, when should you decide your categories?
You observe how students get to school (walk/ride/car). What is the best way to record?
You want to know how many kids in class RIDE bikes to school. Which question works?
options: 'How do you usually get to school?'

items.prompt: Survey the household
items.observeScript: Ask your child to survey the household (or 5 classmates): 'How do you get to school / work?' with 3 categories: walk, car, ride. They prepare a tally sheet, collect the answers, count up each category, and tell you which was most popular and which least.

observeRubric.secure: Sets up categories and tally, collects, counts, answers most/least popular
observeRubric.partial: Collects but counts wrongly, or needs the sheet made for them
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot run the survey process yet even with a modelled example

items.prompt: Which type of graph uses pictures to show data?
On a column graph, a TALLER column means…
Two different displays of the same data should…
options: show the same story in different ways

items.prompt: Which display makes it EASIEST to compare exact numbers?
options: a column graph with a scale

items.prompt: Two displays, one story
items.observeScript: Use your household ice-cream/fruit survey. Have your child make a tally chart AND a simple sticker chart or hand-drawn column graph of the same data. Ask: 'Which was most popular? By how many? Which display is easier to read? Which would you show a teacher?'

observeRubric.secure: Builds both displays, answers most/least and the difference, compares the displays with a reason
observeRubric.partial: Both displays built but comparison/difference needs support
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot build a display without step-by-step help
